title: Does Every User Need a Private LoRA? Decoupling Personalization from Per-User Adaptation

paper.title: Does Every User Need a Private LoRA? Decoupling Personalization from Per-User Adaptation
paper.abstract: Abstract Personalized large language models often require a complete adaptation state for each user. However, this paradigm scales poorly as the user population grows. We revisit this design through the lens of personalization capacity allocation : how much adaptation capacity can be shared across users, how that shared capacity should be composed, and how much adaptation must remain user-specific. We answer these questions through three complementary empirical analyses. We find that independent user adapters contain substantial cross-user reusable structure, that the utility of reusable directions reflects both user relevance and variation across queries, and that user histories provide transferable signals for compact individual correction. Motivated by these findings, we propose LINEUP . It learns a bank of reusable low-rank personalization factors, composes them through user-conditioned recall and query-dependent calibration, and restricts target-user adaptation to a tiny user code over a shared correction space. This design decouples expressive personalization capacity from per-user trainable state. Each target user optimizes only eight scalars, while all shared components remain fixed. By comparison, the evaluated private-LoRA configuration uses 4.19 million per-user parameters. Our theoretical analysis gives a finite-step, finite-history risk bound and sufficient conditions for user-code refinement to improve on history initialization. Across six tasks spanning personalized classification, prediction, and generation, LINEUP leads on all 12 metrics, each averaged over three independent runs (e.g., reducing LaMP-3 RMSE by 11.4% relative to the strongest baseline). It maintains advantages under limited history. These results show that rich personalization can be supported primarily by reusable, conditionally composed shared capacity, while independent user adaptation remains confined to a tiny correction state.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) can acquire task-specific knowledge and behaviors through adaptation ( Chung et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . However, such adaptation is typically learned from data pooled across users and produces a single model shared by the population. It captures what users have in common within a task, but not how their preferences differ. For example, the same input may require different outputs for different users. Personalized Large Language Models (PLLMs) therefore seek to adapt shared models to individual preferences inferred from user histories or feedback ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Recently, PLLMs have received attention in scenarios across text generation, conversation, multimodal generation, and recommender systems ( Trajanovski et al., 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2025b ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . Existing PLLM methods broadly differ in how user information is converted into personalized behavior. Tuning-free approaches incorporate user histories through summaries, retrieval, or inference-time steering ( Richardson et al., 2023 ; Salemi et al., 2024a ; Lv et al., 2026 ) . Their effectiveness depends on the quality of history-derived signals. Learned adaptation-based methods instead encode personalization into parameters or representations. One direction performs individualized adaptation construction : OPPU directly optimizes a user-specific PEFT module ( Tan et al., 2024b ) , PerFit retains a personalized representation intervention alongside a collective shift ( Liu et al., 2026a ) , and P2P uses a population-trained hypernetwork to generate complete personalized adapters from user information ( Tan et al., 2026 ) . Another direction improves reuse through user-derived reusable components , such as pieces, group-level modules, or anchor-derived PEFT modules ( Tan et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2026 ) . These methods improve how individualized adaptation is obtained or reused, but largely retain user-associated adaptation modules as the starting point for organizing personalization. A detailed review of related work is provided in Appendix A . We instead view personalized adaptation through the lens of personalization capacity allocation . Rather than starting from a complete individualized adaptation state, we ask what personalization capacity can be learned directly for cross-user reuse, how this shared capacity should be composed for each request, and how much still must be independently estimated for a target user. This leads to the central question of our work: How much of a personalized adapter is actually personal? We investigate this question through three complementary empirical analyses. 1. Independently learned user adapters contain substantial cross-user reusable structure (Figure 1 (a)). 2. The functional utility of reusable directions exhibits both persistent user association (Figure 1 (b)) and substantial variation across queries from the same user. 3. User histories provide transferable individual correction signals (Figure 1 (c)) that can be preferentially retained in compact shared spaces. Together, these findings suggest organizing personalization around shared capacity, conditional composition, and compact individual correction. Motivated by these findings, we propose LINEUP , which decouples personalization capacity from per-user adaptation. LINEUP directly learns fine-grained low-rank personalization factors across all source-training users as reusable population-level capacity, rather than deriving reusable components from independently learned user adapters. A target user’s history recalls a set of relevant factors. Each query from the same user then calibrates their sparse composition. Remaining individual variation is handled by shared correction maps controlled by a single eight-dimensional user code. The code is initialized from the user’s history and refined using history-derived support examples while all shared components remain fixed. Therefore, rich personalization capacity is learned predominantly through reusable shared structure, while target-user optimization is confined to only eight scalars . By comparison, the evaluated OPPU configuration uses 4.19 million per-user parameters. To characterize this compact adaptation, we derive a finite-step, finite-history risk bound for user-code refinement, linking shared-space approximation and history initialization to fitting progress and support–query disagreement. Across six tasks spanning personalized classification, prediction, and generation, LINEUP leads on all 12 reported metrics, with each reported score averaged over three independent runs. Under cold-start settings, LINEUP maintains clear advantages as the available user history is limited. The scalability analysis shows low incremental per-user storage as the user population grows. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: • We systematically study personalized adaptation from a personalization capacity allocation perspective and identify three properties: cross-user reuse, user- and query-dependent composition, and transferable individual correction. • We derive a finite-step, finite-history risk bound for regularized user-code refinement and establish sufficient conditions for improvement over history initialization. • We propose LINEUP , which decouples personalization capacity from per-user adaptation. It achieves the best mean performance on various personalization tasks while reducing parameter and storage growth, with further benefits under cold-start settings.

sections.heading: 2.1 Personalization Problem Setup
sections.text: We study each personalized task 𝒯 \mathcal{T} independently, with input space 𝒳 𝒯 \mathcal{X}_{\mathcal{T}} and output space 𝒴 𝒯 \mathcal{Y}_{\mathcal{T}} . Source users provide data for learning population-shared personalization components, while target users are unseen during shared training and are personalized only from their own available history. Following LaMP and OPPU ( Salemi et al., 2024b ; Tan et al., 2024b ) , history records are input–output pairs. Personalization may use ℋ u \mathcal{H}_{u} and the current query x x , but never its target output y y . sections.heading: 3 Empirical Analysis of Personalized Adaptation
sections.text: We examine how personalization capacity can be shared, composed, and individually corrected. RQ1 and RQ2 analyze independently optimized OPPU adapters ( Tan et al., 2024b ) on a fixed LLM backbone; RQ3 studies representation corrections without user adapters. Unless stated otherwise, intervals are 95% user-level bootstrap confidence intervals. See Appendix B for detailed mathematical definitions and supporting evidence. Dataset details are provided in Section 5.1 . The design choices informed by these analyses are evaluated through ablations in Section 5.5 .

sections.heading: 3.1 RQ1: How Much Structure Is Reusable across User Adapters?
sections.text: Observation 1 (Sharing). Independently trained user adapters share substantial structure: a small subspace learned from other users captures much of held-out update energy. We here learn common output directions from one group of users and test how much of other users’ adapter-update energy they capture. We compare these directions with random subspaces of the same dimension on LaMP-2M, LaMP-2N, LaMP-5, and LaMP-7 datasets. Figure 1 (a) shows that 32 directions (0.8% of the output dimension) capture 54.1%–67.9% of held-out update energy, versus 0.78% for random subspaces. Removing task-adapter output directions barely changes coverage. Size-matched random-partition bases also capture substantial energy, but genuine-user bases cover 14.3–21.0 percentage points more on the same updates (Appendix B.1 ). These findings motivate jointly learning reusable personalization factors rather than duplicating shared structure in user adapters.

sections.heading: 3.2 RQ2: How Does Direction Utility Vary across Users and Queries?
sections.text: Observation 2 (Composing). The utility of reusable directions exhibits persistent user-associated structure and substantial variation across queries from the same user. Are reusable directions equally useful for every request? On LaMP-2M and LaMP-2N, we keep each user’s adapter fixed and measure the first-order change in query loss induced by strengthening each of eight shared directions. Comparing these signed responses within and across users tests whether their utility reflects recurring user patterns, request-specific needs, or both. Figure 1 (b) shows higher within-user than cross-user Spearman agreement: 0.145 versus 0.008 on LaMP-2M and 0.400 versus 0.059 on LaMP-2N. This within-user advantage holds across all analyzed layers and projections (Appendix B.2.2 ). Yet differences between a user’s queries still account for 82.7% and 61.3% of response variation after controlling for overall sensitivity scale (Appendix B.2.3 ). Direction-removal checks further show that the sensitivities closely track actual loss changes (Appendix B.2.4 ). Together, these results suggest a hierarchical technique where history-conditioned candidate recall is followed by query-dependent calibration.

sections.heading: 3.3 RQ3: Can User History Guide Compact Individual Correction?
sections.text: Observation 3 (Correcting). User histories provide transferable correction after removing average label-response directions, and compact shared spaces preferentially retain it. We now ask whether correction inferred from a user’s history transfers to new queries, measured by alignment with their first-order loss-reducing directions. On LaMP-2M and LaMP-2N, we control shared label structure by removing the span of average label responses from both history and query correction signals. We compare own history with random and label-matched donor histories and evaluate compact spaces learned only from other users’ histories (Appendix B.3 ). Figure 1 (c) shows positive own-history transfer, with intervals excluding zero and means above those of both donor conditions. Own-history point estimates are positive at all eight analyzed layers on both tasks (Appendix B.3.2 ). First-order intervention checks support the loss-based interpretation of this alignment (Appendix B.3.4 ). An eight-dimensional space per layer retains 34.7% and 29.4% of full-space own-history transfer on LaMP-2M and LaMP-2N, respectively, while capturing only 12.9% and 17.0% of residual query-correction energy (Figure 6 (a)). Compact spaces therefore preserve a larger fraction of useful transfer than of correction energy. This motivates shared correction maps with compact, history-fitted user coordinates, complementing conditional factor composition.

sections.heading: 4.1 Fine-Grained Shared Personalization Factors
sections.text: Observation 1 motivates changing the unit of personalization from complete user adapters to reusable factors. LINEUP jointly learns its factor bank across all source-training users under conditional composition, rather than extracting components from separately trained user adapters. Each factor can serve multiple users without representing any one user in full. This allows factors to specialize as complementary personalization units, while overlapping subsets produce distinct personalized updates (Appendix C.2 ).

sections.heading: 4.3 History-Initialized Adaptation with Tiny User Codes
sections.text: Different users can draw on the same personalization factors while requiring different combinations of them. LINEUP therefore places its main personalization capacity in shared factor composition, while a tiny user code addresses individual differences that this composition does not fully capture. Observation 3 motivates sharing correction capabilities while adapting only their user-specific coordinates. Shared maps learn how to correct representations. A single eight-dimensional code specifies the user’s correction. It is initialized from a population-informed starting point, and support fitting adjusts it using individual evidence. The same fitted code coordinates corrections across layers and is reused across queries, rather than introducing independently learned user matrices (Appendix C.3 ). Learning shared capacity. We first train S1 across source users, then freeze it and learn the shared correction maps and initializer using initialized codes. S1 remains active during both shared S2 training and target-user code fitting. At personalization time, only the code is updated. The LLM backbone remains frozen throughout (Algorithm 1 ).

sections.heading: 4.4 Theoretical Analysis of Compact User Adaptation
sections.text: We analyze S2’s regularized, finite-step Adam fitting with S1 active and all shared parameters fixed. Under the conditions in Appendix D , our risk bound relates shared-space approximation and history-initialization error to fitting progress and support–query disagreement. It gives a sufficient condition for support fitting to improve on initialization, while accounting for history reuse (Corollary 1 ). A deterministic bound on code displacement supports this finite-step analysis without requiring convergence (Lemma 1 ). The risk bound separates shared-space approximation from code-space estimation, while accounting for shared geometry and stability. A complementary quadratic analysis explains when remaining correction need outweighs estimation noise (Corollary 2 ). Together, these results support learning rich correction capabilities jointly while keeping individual fitting compact.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets and metrics. We evaluate LINEUP on six tasks of the LaMP personalization benchmark ( Salemi et al., 2024b ) , spanning classification, rating prediction, and generation. We follow OPPU’s data processing and target-user protocol, keeping source and target users disjoint. We report Accuracy and Macro-F1 for LaMP-2M/2N, mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean square error (RMSE) for LaMP-3, and ROUGE-1/ROUGE-L for generation. Lower is better for MAE and RMSE; higher is better otherwise. Dataset and metric details appear in Appendix E.1 – E.2 . Baselines. We compare LINEUP against eight baselines. Non uses the pretrained LLM backbone without task adaptation or personalization. Basic applies task adaptation without per-user personalization. RAG augments the task-adapted model’s input with retrieved user history. OPPU ( Tan et al., 2024b ) learns a private adapter for each user, while PerFit ( Liu et al., 2026a ) learns collective and user-specific representation shifts. Per-Pcs ( Tan et al., 2024a ) assembles reusable pieces of user adapters. P2P ( Tan et al., 2026 ) trains a shared hypernetwork across source users to generate adapters from user profiles and retrieved history. MTA ( Li et al., 2026 ) merges anchor-user adapters before individual refinement. Details appear in Appendix E.3 . Implementation details. We use Llama-2-7B as the base model to align with most baselines’ released code. LINEUP builds on OPPU’s non-personalized task-adapted backbone and learns shared components separately. sections.heading: 5.2 Main Results on LaMP
sections.text: Tables 1 and 2 show that LINEUP achieves the best mean performance on all 12 metrics across six tasks . Representative gains include a 0.020 0.020 F1 improvement over PerFit on LaMP-2M, a 0.050 0.050 RMSE reduction on LaMP-3, and a 0.029 0.029 improvement in ROUGE-L over OPPU on LaMP-7. While the strongest baseline varies across tasks, LINEUP consistently leads across tasks. Effectively organizing shared capacity around reusable factors. OPPU and PerFit retain individual adaptation states, while Per-Pcs and MTA reuse components derived from user adapters. Our comparison also includes cross-user, history-conditioned learning through P2P’s population-trained hypernetwork. RQ 1 indicates that separate states repeatedly devote limited capacity to common structure. LINEUP jointly learns factors for user- and query-conditioned composition, allowing overlapping subsets to serve different users and requests without retraining. Its distinction lies in organizing shared capacity around reusable factors while restricting independent adaptation to compact correction. The consistent gains support this factor-centric capacity-allocation strategy as a whole, combining shared learning, conditional composition, and compact individual refinement. Reserving individual adaptation for compact correction. RQ 3 reveals that user histories provide transferable correction signals that compact shared spaces can preferentially retain. Section 4.4 shows how finite-step fitting can improve history initialization when its progress outweighs support–query disagreement, with statistical complexity controlled in the user-code space. LINEUP therefore places most modeling capacity in shared structures and reserves a lightweight code for targeted individual correction. The results support this division of labor: shared capacity and compact individual correction together yield stronger personalization without a full private adaptation state per user.

Cold-start scenarios are common in real-world PLLM deployment, where personalization must begin with limited user history. We therefore evaluate how effectively LINEUP personalizes unseen target users as the amount of available history is restricted. We vary the available history of unseen target users while keeping users and evaluation queries fixed. On LaMP-2N, LINEUP achieves the best mean Accuracy and the best or tied-best reported Macro-F1 across history budgets (Figure 3 (a–b)). The detailed protocol and complementary generation task results on LaMP-4 appear in Appendix F.2 . Rich shared capacity from minimal history. Our factor bank learns reusable personalization patterns across source users before target-user adaptation. Available history provides cues for recalling relevant factors, rather than requiring these patterns to be relearned for each user. It indicates that our shared factors already supply much of the needed personalization. The tiny user code then addresses residual individual differences not fully captured by factor composition. Concentrating independent estimation on this correction also aligns with the finite-history risk analysis in Section 4.4 .

sections.heading: 5.4 Efficiency and Scalability
sections.text: Most benchmark tasks in our evaluation involve about 100 target users, whereas real-world PLLM services may serve far larger populations. Adaptation storage thereby becomes a vital constraint for multi-adapter deployment ( Abdelzaher et al., 2025 ) . Figure 3 (c) shows analytical storage scaling for the evaluated LaMP-2N configurations, normalized to bf16: LINEUP adds only 16 B per user. LINEUP’s total adaptation storage becomes lower than OPPU’s at 17 users and PerFit’s at 95 users. Both thresholds are very small for large-scale services, where LINEUP’s storage savings over these baselines grow with the user population. At 1,024 users, the projected totals, including shared parameters, are approximately 151.2 MB for LINEUP, 1.61 GB for PerFit, and 8.60 GB for OPPU. Accounting details and comparisons with Per-Pcs and MTA appear in Appendix F.3 . Amortizing shared capacity across users. In OPPU, each private adapter must accommodate both reusable patterns and individual variation, while overlapping structure is repeatedly learned and stored across users ( RQ 1 ). LINEUP instead invests in a larger factor bank jointly learned across source users, providing more capacity to capture diverse reusable personalization patterns. Only residual individual correction requires an eight-dimensional code. This organization explains how richer personalization and lower storage can coexist. Capacity is thus expanded where it can be shared, rather than replicated in every user module. MTA also reuses components but retains large individualized adapters, leaving substantial per-user storage growth (Figure 7 (c)). Compact per-request activation. History-conditioned recall and query calibration allow each request to draw on only a small part of the shared bank. Each request activates four rank-4 factors from the 32-factor bank, yielding a combined update of rank at most 16 at each adapted projection. The larger bank therefore expands the range of reusable personalization patterns without requiring its full capacity to be activated for every request. sections.heading: 5.5 Ablation Studies
sections.text: We conduct an ablation study across representative tasks (LaMP-2M and LaMP-5) to validate our three design choices of LINEUP: history-guided factor retrieval, query-conditioned composition, and the tiny user-specific correction. The ablation protocol is provided in Appendix F.4 . For the two routing ablations, S1-only is the reference. Random candidates replaces history-guided recall with a fixed random subset of the same size for each user, while preserving history- and query-based scoring within the candidate set. No query calibration removes the query contribution during training and inference while retaining history-conditioned recall. To examine S2, we consider three variants. S1 only omits the entire correction mechanism, while S1 + initialized code applies history-initialized correction without support fitting. Full LINEUP uses the same shared checkpoints and further refines the code on history-derived support examples. Table 3 shows that random candidates cause the largest degradation relative to S1-only, while removing query calibration also reduces performance on both tasks. Full LINEUP outperforms S1-only, supporting S2 as a whole. On all four metrics, shared correction maps with history-based initialization improve mean performance over S1-only, and support fitting adds further gains. These results support both routing choices within the factor bank and refinement beyond initialized correction. A code-dimension sweep further shows that increasing r c r_{c} from 2 to 8 improves mean performance, while larger codes yield no consistent additional gains across metrics (Appendix F.5 ).

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: We revisited personalized adaptation through the lens of personalization capacity allocation and conducted three empirical analyses. Our findings motivated LINEUP, which directly learns fine-grained reusable factors across users, composes them using user history and the current query, and confines user-specific fitting to a compact residual correction. Our theoretical analysis bounds the risk of finite-step code refinement under limited history. Across six LaMP tasks, LINEUP achieves the best mean performance while optimizing only eight scalars per target user, with clear advantages under limited history and low incremental parameter and storage costs. These results show that rich personalization need not require a full private adapter for every user. Shared learning and conditional composition provide rich personalization capacity, while independent user adaptation is reserved for compact individual correction. Future work will extend this task-isolated formulation to cross-task personalization, capturing stable user preferences through reusable factors.

sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI tools, including ChatGPT ( https://chatgpt.com/ ) and Claude ( https://claude.ai/ ), to assist with polishing the writing. sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: Personalized large language models raise privacy, bias, and resource concerns because they rely on user-specific histories and adaptation states. First, LINEUP replaces complete private adapters with eight-dimensional user codes, substantially reducing the persistent user-specific model state that must be stored and protected. This compact design can simplify personalized-parameter management. User histories, codes, and shared components still require appropriate access controls and privacy safeguards. Second, history-based personalization may reflect biases or manipulation in user data. LINEUP’s separation of shared components and individual codes offers a basis for targeted auditing. Output review and transparent user controls can help address undesirable personalization and support responsible use. Third, LLM training and inference entail computational and environmental costs. By reusing shared personalization capacity rather than maintaining a complete adapter for every user, LINEUP substantially reduces per-user parameter and storage requirements, supporting more resource-efficient personalization as the user population grows.

sections.heading: A.1 Personalized Large Language Models
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across language understanding and generation ( Li et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Sui et al., 2025 ; Le-Cong et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . Personalized large language models adapt model behavior to individual users based on their histories, profiles, or preference feedback ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Existing methods can be broadly grouped into tuning-free, learned adaptation-based, and alignment approaches. Tuning-free personalization. Tuning-free methods typically summarize or retrieve user histories to construct personalized prompts or augment the model context ( Richardson et al., 2023 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Salemi et al., 2024a ; Zerhoudi and Granitzer, 2026 ) . Other approaches steer generation at inference time by contrasting personalized and non-personalized model states or combining decoding signals ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Lv et al., 2026 ) . These methods avoid target-user parameter optimization and can readily incorporate newly available histories. However, their effectiveness depends on the quality of historical data preprocessing. Learned adaptation-based personalization. This is a complementary family that encodes personalization into learned parameters or representation-space interventions. We organize them according to the basic adaptation unit from which target-user personalization is constructed. The first direction performs individualized adaptation construction . OPPU directly optimizes an independent PEFT module for each user by using their history ( Tan et al., 2024b ) . PerFit decomposes representation-space personalization into collective and personalized shifts while retaining a user-specific intervention for individual variation ( Liu et al., 2026a ) . P2P changes how such individualized adaptation is obtained by introducing a population-trained hypernetwork. It maps a user profile gained during preprocessing and the user’s query-retrieved history to a complete set of personalized LoRA parameters. P2P thereby avoids iterative per-user fine-tuning at deployment ( Tan et al., 2026 ) . Despite these differences, the primary personalization object remains an individualized adaptation module that can be optimized directly, instantiated in representation space, or generated from user information. Methods that fit and retain such modules incur user-specific optimization and persistent-state costs, while hypernetwork generation shifts part of this burden to preprocessing stages. Thus, these approaches mainly improve how an individualized adaptation state is obtained, rather than changing the granularity at which personalization capacity itself is organized. The second direction improves reuse through user-derived reusable components . Per-Pcs learns personalized PEFT modules for selected users, decomposes them into reusable pieces, and assembles pieces for target users ( Tan et al., 2024a ) . PROPER introduces intermediate group-level adaptation and combines group LoRAs with individual user LoRAs ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) . MTA constructs a bank of anchor-derived Meta-LoRAs, retrieves and merges relevant modules for a target user, and additionally fits an individual LoRA for few-shot refinement ( Li et al., 2026 ) . These approaches demonstrate the value of cross-user reuse. Nevertheless, their reusable units are obtained from adaptation modules associated with particular users. Their emphasis is on reusing such modules, rather than systematically characterizing what structure is reusable. This leaves open a different organization of personalization capacity: whether reusable units can instead be learned directly as cross-user personalization factors and composed according to the current request. Personalized alignment. Personalized alignment forms a complementary line of research that typically models personalization through heterogeneous objectives or preference signals. User preferences can be incorporated through personalized reward modeling, parameter merging, or decoding-time policy combination ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Rame et al., 2023 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025a ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . These methods usually assume explicit preference feedback or a predefined preference space. By contrast, our setting focuses on task-specific personalization inferred from heterogeneous behavioral histories, where user-specific behavior must be recovered from prior interactions rather than supplied as an explicit alignment objective. Positioning of our work. We take personalization capacity allocation as the organizing principle. The central distinction is not whether parameters are shared across users, but what is shared, how reusable capacity is learned, and what must still be independently adapted for a target user . LINEUP differs from individualized adaptation methods by changing the basic personalization unit. Rather than constructing a complete adaptation state for each user or request, it directly learns fine-grained low-rank personalization factors across source users as reusable population-level capacity. Different users can reuse overlapping factors, while the same user can employ different compositions for different requests. LINEUP also differs from collaborative adapter-reuse methods in the origin of this reusable capacity, since its factor bank is learned jointly for cross-user composition from the outset, rather than being obtained by first learning user-, anchor-, or group-associated adapters and subsequently decomposing, selecting, or merging them. Our composition mechanism further separates persistent user relevance from request-specific utility. A user’s history first recalls a compact candidate set of factors, and the current query then calibrates their sparse selection and mixture. LINEUP further confines target-user optimization to an eight-dimensional code over shared correction maps. Therefore, most personalization capacity resides in reusable shared structures, while only a tiny coordinate state must be independently estimated for a new target user. This factor-centric design is motivated by our empirical findings. Taken together, LINEUP decouples personalization capacity from per-user adaptation : expressive personalization is learned predominantly through reusable, conditionally composed shared capacity, whereas independent target-user fitting is reserved for a compact residual correction. This organization simultaneously targets strong personalization, adaptation from limited user history, and low incremental parameter and storage cost as the user population grows.

sections.heading: A.2 Mixture of Experts
sections.text: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine specialized expert modules through learned routing mechanisms ( Jacobs et al., 1991 ; Cai et al., 2025 ) . Sparse MoE activates only a subset of experts for each input, enabling specialized and compositional model capacity without proportional computation ( Shazeer et al., 2017 ; Du et al., 2022 ; Dai et al., 2024 ) . Beyond general-purpose model scaling, MoE-style architectures have also been studied in decentralized collaborative training and personalized federated learning ( Liu et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Yi et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . In much of this literature, personalization is defined at the client level, with shared or private experts introduced to accommodate heterogeneity in local data distributions, model architectures, or computational resources ( Tan et al., 2023 ; Sabah et al., 2024 ) . Personalized LLMs focus on a different problem where the model must infer latent individual preferences from behavioral histories and tailor its behavior jointly to the user and the current request. LINEUP adopts the compositional principle of sparse expert models but uses it for a different granularity and purpose. Its experts are fine-grained low-rank personalization factors jointly learned as reusable cross-user capacity, rather than independently meaningful user or client models. No single factor is intended to represent a complete user. Instead, different users can reuse overlapping factors, and personalization emerges from their conditional composition. Routing is explicitly hierarchical, where user history first narrows the shared factor bank to a candidate set, after which the current query calibrates candidate factors. This separates persistent user relevance from request-specific utility rather than collapsing both into a single routing decision. LINEUP therefore uses expert-style composition as part of a broader personalization capacity allocation strategy, rather than as a conventional mechanism for model scaling or client specialization.

sections.text: The finite-step NLL bounds use the stated smoothness and influence conditions, not Adam convergence. sections.heading: E.3 Baselines
sections.text: We use baselines’ official implementations. Their personalization algorithms are retained under the common Llama-2-7B backbone and OPPU target-user protocol. Source-data construction and shared training remain method-specific to ensure fairness. OPPU and PerFit perform task adaptation on the full source pool. P2P trains its hypernetwork on all source users, conditioning adapter generation on user profiles and query-retrieved history. Per-Pcs and MTA retain their released selection procedures, choosing sharers or anchors from up to 1,000 candidates drawn from the full source partition. RAG retrieves the top user-history record using BM25. Per-Pcs and MTA provide no complete released configuration for LaMP-2N. MTA also excludes LaMP-7 because its adaptation-data construction requires query–answer pairs. These entries are marked as NA.

sections.text: We learn LINEUP’s shared components on source-training users and select hyperparameters on source-validation users. Selection uses the arithmetic mean of the two task metrics, maximized for classification and generation and minimized for LaMP-3. The selected configurations are fixed before final target-user evaluation. We report mean ± \pm standard deviation over three runs. LINEUP and baselines are independently trained with three seeds.

sections.text: The displayed curves begin at 100 users, reflecting the approximately 100 target users in most tasks under our evaluation protocol. For LaMP-2N, LINEUP becomes more storage-efficient than OPPU at 17 users and PerFit at 95 users, while remaining below P2P’s 615.33 MB shared state over the displayed range. At LaMP-2N’s actual evaluation size of 49 target users, PerFit therefore has lower total adaptation storage than LINEUP. However, this paradigm scales poorly as the user population grows. We revisit this design through the lens of personalization capacity allocation : how much adaptation capacity can be shared across users, how that shared capacity should be composed, and how much adaptation must remain user-specific. We answer these questions through three complementary empirical analyses. We find that independent user adapters contain substantial cross-user reusable structure, that the utility of reusable directions reflects both user relevance and variation across queries, and that user histories provide transferable signals for compact individual correction. Motivated by these findings, we propose LINEUP . It learns a bank of reusable low-rank personalization factors, composes them through user-conditioned recall and query-dependent calibration, and restricts target-user adaptation to a tiny user code over a shared correction space. This design decouples expressive personalization capacity from per-user trainable state. Each target user optimizes only eight scalars, while all shared components remain fixed. By comparison, the evaluated private-LoRA configuration uses 4.19 million per-user parameters. Our theoretical analysis gives a finite-step, finite-history risk bound and sufficient conditions for user-code refinement to improve on history initialization. Across six tasks spanning personalized classification, prediction, and generation, LINEUP leads on all 12 metrics, each averaged over three independent runs (e.g., reducing LaMP-3 RMSE by 11.4% relative to the strongest baseline). It maintains advantages under limited history. These results show that rich personalization can be supported primarily by reusable, conditionally composed shared capacity, while independent user adaptation remains confined to a tiny correction state. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) can acquire task-specific knowledge and behaviors through adaptation ( Chung et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . However, such adaptation is typically learned from data pooled across users and produces a single model shared by the population. It captures what users have in common within a task, but not how their preferences differ. For example, the same input may require different outputs for different users. Personalized Large Language Models (PLLMs) therefore seek to adapt shared models to individual preferences inferred from user histories or feedback ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Recently, PLLMs have received attention in scenarios across text generation, conversation, multimodal generation, and recommender systems ( Trajanovski et al., 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2025b ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . Existing PLLM methods broadly differ in how user information is converted into personalized behavior. Tuning-free approaches incorporate user histories through summaries, retrieval, or inference-time steering ( Richardson et al., 2023 ; Salemi et al., 2024a ; Lv et al., 2026 ) . Their effectiveness depends on the quality of history-derived signals. Learned adaptation-based methods instead encode personalization into parameters or representations. One direction performs individualized adaptation construction : OPPU directly optimizes a user-specific PEFT module ( Tan et al., 2024b ) , PerFit retains a personalized representation intervention alongside a collective shift ( Liu et al., 2026a ) , and P2P uses a population-trained hypernetwork to generate complete personalized adapters from user information ( Tan et al., 2026 ) . Another direction improves reuse through user-derived reusable components , such as pieces, group-level modules, or anchor-derived PEFT modules ( Tan et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2026 ) . These methods improve how individualized adaptation is obtained or reused, but largely retain user-associated adaptation modules as the starting point for organizing personalization. A detailed review of related work is provided in Appendix A . We instead view personalized adaptation through the lens of personalization capacity allocation . Rather than starting from a complete individualized adaptation state, we ask what personalization capacity can be learned directly for cross-user reuse, how this shared capacity should be composed for each request, and how much still must be independently estimated for a target user. This leads to the central question of our work: How much of a personalized adapter is actually personal? We investigate this question through three complementary empirical analyses. 1. Independently learned user adapters contain substantial cross-user reusable structure (Figure 1 (a)). 2. The functional utility of reusable directions exhibits both persistent user association (Figure 1 (b)) and substantial variation across queries from the same user. 3. User histories provide transferable individual correction signals (Figure 1 (c)) that can be preferentially retained in compact shared spaces. Together, these findings suggest organizing personalization around shared capacity, conditional composition, and compact individual correction. Motivated by these findings, we propose LINEUP , which decouples personalization capacity from per-user adaptation. LINEUP directly learns fine-grained low-rank personalization factors across all source-training users as reusable population-level capacity, rather than deriving reusable components from independently learned user adapters. A target user’s history recalls a set of relevant factors. Each query from the same user then calibrates their sparse composition. Remaining individual variation is handled by shared correction maps controlled by a single eight-dimensional user code. The code is initialized from the user’s history and refined using history-derived support examples while all shared components remain fixed. Therefore, rich personalization capacity is learned predominantly through reusable shared structure, while target-user optimization is confined to only eight scalars . By comparison, the evaluated OPPU configuration uses 4.19 million per-user parameters. To characterize this compact adaptation, we derive a finite-step, finite-history risk bound for user-code refinement, linking shared-space approximation and history initialization to fitting progress and support–query disagreement. Across six tasks spanning personalized classification, prediction, and generation, LINEUP leads on all 12 reported metrics, with each reported score averaged over three independent runs. Under cold-start settings, LINEUP maintains clear advantages as the available user history is limited. The scalability analysis shows low incremental per-user storage as the user population grows. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: • We systematically study personalized adaptation from a personalization capacity allocation perspective and identify three properties: cross-user reuse, user- and query-dependent composition, and transferable individual correction. • We derive a finite-step, finite-history risk bound for regularized user-code refinement and establish sufficient conditions for improvement over history initialization. • We propose LINEUP , which decouples personalization capacity from per-user adaptation. Independently trained user adapters share substantial structure: a small subspace learned from other users captures much of held-out update energy. We here learn common output directions from one group of users and test how much of other users’ adapter-update energy they capture. We compare these directions with random subspaces of the same dimension on LaMP-2M, LaMP-2N, LaMP-5, and LaMP-7 datasets. Figure 1 (a) shows that 32 directions (0.8% of the output dimension) capture 54.1%–67.9% of held-out update energy, versus 0.78% for random subspaces. Removing task-adapter output directions barely changes coverage. Size-matched random-partition bases also capture substantial energy, but genuine-user bases cover 14.3–21.0 percentage points more on the same updates (Appendix B.1 ). These findings motivate jointly learning reusable personalization factors rather than duplicating shared structure in user adapters. 3.2 RQ2: How Does Direction Utility Vary across Users and Queries? Observation 2 (Composing). The utility of reusable directions exhibits persistent user-associated structure and substantial variation across queries from the same user. Are reusable directions equally useful for every request? On LaMP-2M and LaMP-2N, we keep each user’s adapter fixed and measure the first-order change in query loss induced by strengthening each of eight shared directions. Comparing these signed responses within and across users tests whether their utility reflects recurring user patterns, request-specific needs, or both. Figure 1 (b) shows higher within-user than cross-user Spearman agreement: 0.145 versus 0.008 on LaMP-2M and 0.400 versus 0.059 on LaMP-2N. This within-user advantage holds across all analyzed layers and projections (Appendix B.2.2 ). Yet differences between a user’s queries still account for 82.7% and 61.3% of response variation after controlling for overall sensitivity scale (Appendix B.2.3 ). Direction-removal checks further show that the sensitivities closely track actual loss changes (Appendix B.2.4 ). Together, these results suggest a hierarchical technique where history-conditioned candidate recall is followed by query-dependent calibration. 3.3 RQ3: Can User History Guide Compact Individual Correction? Observation 3 (Correcting). User histories provide transferable correction after removing average label-response directions, and compact shared spaces preferentially retain it. We now ask whether correction inferred from a user’s history transfers to new queries, measured by alignment with their first-order loss-reducing directions. On LaMP-2M and LaMP-2N, we control shared label structure by removing the span of average label responses from both history and query correction signals. We compare own history with random and label-matched donor histories and evaluate compact spaces learned only from other users’ histories (Appendix B.3 ). Figure 1 (c) shows positive own-history transfer, with intervals excluding zero and means above those of both donor conditions. Own-history point estimates are positive at all eight analyzed layers on both tasks (Appendix B.3.2 ). First-order intervention checks support the loss-based interpretation of this alignment (Appendix B.3.4 ). An eight-dimensional space per layer retains 34.7% and 29.4% of full-space own-history transfer on LaMP-2M and LaMP-2N, respectively, while capturing only 12.9% and 17.0% of residual query-correction energy (Figure 6 (a)). Compact spaces therefore preserve a larger fraction of useful transfer than of correction energy. While the strongest baseline varies across tasks, LINEUP consistently leads across tasks. Effectively organizing shared capacity around reusable factors. OPPU and PerFit retain individual adaptation states, while Per-Pcs and MTA reuse components derived from user adapters. Our comparison also includes cross-user, history-conditioned learning through P2P’s population-trained hypernetwork. RQ 1 indicates that separate states repeatedly devote limited capacity to common structure. LINEUP jointly learns factors for user- and query-conditioned composition, allowing overlapping subsets to serve different users and requests without retraining. Its distinction lies in organizing shared capacity around reusable factors while restricting independent adaptation to compact correction. The consistent gains support this factor-centric capacity-allocation strategy as a whole, combining shared learning, conditional composition, and compact individual refinement. Reserving individual adaptation for compact correction. RQ 3 reveals that user histories provide transferable correction signals that compact shared spaces can preferentially retain. Section 4.4 shows how finite-step fitting can improve history initialization when its progress outweighs support–query disagreement, with statistical complexity controlled in the user-code space. LINEUP therefore places most modeling capacity in shared structures and reserves a lightweight code for targeted individual correction. Accounting details and comparisons with Per-Pcs and MTA appear in Appendix F.3 . Amortizing shared capacity across users. In OPPU, each private adapter must accommodate both reusable patterns and individual variation, while overlapping structure is repeatedly learned and stored across users ( RQ 1 ). LINEUP instead invests in a larger factor bank jointly learned across source users, providing more capacity to capture diverse reusable personalization patterns. Only residual individual correction requires an eight-dimensional code. This organization explains how richer personalization and lower storage can coexist. Capacity is thus expanded where it can be shared, rather than replicated in every user module. MTA also reuses components but retains large individualized adapters, leaving substantial per-user storage growth (Figure 7 (c)). Compact per-request activation. History-conditioned recall and query calibration allow each request to draw on only a small part of the shared bank. Each request activates four rank-4 factors from the 32-factor bank, yielding a combined update of rank at most 16 at each adapted projection. The larger bank therefore expands the range of reusable personalization patterns without requiring its full capacity to be activated for every request. Our findings motivated LINEUP, which directly learns fine-grained reusable factors across users, composes them using user history and the current query, and confines user-specific fitting to a compact residual correction. Our theoretical analysis bounds the risk of finite-step code refinement under limited history. Across six LaMP tasks, LINEUP achieves the best mean performance while optimizing only eight scalars per target user, with clear advantages under limited history and low incremental parameter and storage costs. These results show that rich personalization need not require a full private adapter for every user. Shared learning and conditional composition provide rich personalization capacity, while independent user adaptation is reserved for compact individual correction. Future work will extend this task-isolated formulation to cross-task personalization, capturing stable user preferences through reusable factors. Ethics statement Personalized large language models raise privacy, bias, and resource concerns because they rely on user-specific histories and adaptation states. First, LINEUP replaces complete private adapters with eight-dimensional user codes, substantially reducing the persistent user-specific model state that must be stored and protected. This compact design can simplify personalized-parameter management. User histories, codes, and shared components still require appropriate access controls and privacy safeguards.
